title: The Splinter in the Sky
rationale: Root-down: Speculative fiction -> Science fiction -> Futurist -> Spacefaring fiction -> New space opera -> Political space opera -> Interstellar court politics. Interplanetary imperial court, diplomatic rivalry and a recruited double agent are the engine. Independence and sibling rescue motivate the spy, but elite networks and court negotiation do the political work, not a mass revolt, collapse succession or religious pilgrimage. Soft SF confirmed by publisher and reviewers; no magic.

reason: Parent queued Uncanny thresholds vs Unholy halls ruling.

title: The Strange
rationale: Root-down: Speculative fiction -> Science fiction -> Historical -> Alternate history -> Deep alterations. Explicit alternate 1930s Mars and colonization since the Civil War make an enduring changed world, not a single era marvel. Anabelle crosses the Martian frontier to recover her mothers voice recording. Old Mars is a strong furniture match (breathable Mars, clanking robots, saucers); its Atemporal root fails the usable Earth-time anchor. Space western has the same historical-root conflict. Root-down rule governs, no exception invented.

title: The Tapestry of Time
rationale: Root-down: Speculative fiction -> Fantasy -> Real earth fantasy -> Historical fantasy -> Period fantasy -> Industrial age fantasy -> WWII fantasy. Four British sisters inherit second sight; WWII Resistance missions and Nazi pursuit of the Bayeux Tapestry form the magic-bearing historical stage. Locus explicitly distinguishes family clairvoyance fantasy from psionic SF. No altered-history fork or scientific time travel: visions and an empowering artifact, not era crossing. Family relation is important but contemporary Domestic fantasy fails the wartime historical gate.

title: The Thick and the Lean
rationale: Root-down: Speculative fiction -> Science fiction -> Futurist -> Spacefaring fiction -> Space dystopias. Human colony on an alien two-moon planet: religious and corporate purity culture makes eating taboo, appetite pills and implants police bodies, and class/caste structure constrains chef and cyberthief. Off-Earth oppressive social order is the engine. Earth-future social dystopia fails location; Hard SF, alien contact and rule-making fabulation are not the governing experience. Embedded Kitchen Girl is a book read by characters, not a textual breach.

title: The Thing in the Snow
rationale: Root-down: SF -> Atemporal -> Fabulation -> Classic fabulation -> Absurdist constructed realities. The Northern Institute is an impossible sealed institution that defines its caretakers' reality through pointless weekly maintenance rituals. Adams explicitly says its location cannot exist; snow sickness, the unknown object and managerial psychosis resist scientific resolution. No dated future, literal magic system, textual breach or game-master: the institution is the world-making condition.

title: The Thousand Earths
rationale: Root-down: SF -> Atemporal -> Time travel fiction -> Hard time travel. Relativistic time dilation makes Hackett's starship voyages temporal expeditions: five million years elapse on the first return and vastly longer journeys reveal humanity's and the cosmos's fate. Orion explicitly names him a time traveller. The physical mechanism is central, not an unexplained slip, biological disorder, agency or privately invented time machine; ship travel causes the differential rather than static regions running at unequal rates. The futurist setting therefore yields to the standing any-time-travel gate.

title: The Unbalancing
rationale: Root-down: Fantasy -> Fantasy realms -> Romantasy. Poet Lilun and starkeeper Ranra fall in love while trying to save Gelle-Geu from its unstable underwater star; publisher expressly centers new love and their alternating intimate arcs are co-equal with the catastrophe. Deepnames supply rule-bound collective magic, but the romantic relationship is the plot's spine, not a technical system-solving epic alone. Neither an inherited real-Earth mythology nor cozy safety: invented Birdverse cosmology with bittersweet disaster. Birdverse is a shared setting with different protagonists, not one continuous series card.

title: The Underhistory
rationale: Root-down: SF -> Historical -> Alternate history -> Period alterations -> Alt postwar. In 1941 a plane intentionally crashes into Sinclair House, killing the Australian PM and his wife; main action is in 1993 as survivor Pera confronts escaped convicts. Ian Mond explicitly identifies the PM's impossible death as the sole speculative element. A WWII-era fork depicted after the war, within a lifetime, fits Alt postwar; no real ghosts or supernatural house, so Gothic atmosphere is not Fantasy. The divergence is not an enduring transformed-world premise.

title: The Underwood Tapes
rationale: Root-down: SF -> Atemporal -> Time travel fiction -> Timeslips -> Time bleeds. Present-day Grace and Jake in 1992 communicate by recorded cassettes; no one travels. Kirkus explicitly says the communication exists without explanation. The ordinary tapes are a medium, not an invented time apparatus, and no ritual or magical cause is given. A mystery and grief unfold through the leak between eras, not a stranger's life in another century.

title: The Unmothers
rationale: Root-down: Fantasy -> Real earth fantasy -> Nocturne -> Dark -> Horror -> Folk horror. A grieving reporter enters rural Raeford after a horse bears a human baby, and finds the community's deeply held supernatural secrets, reproductive control and feminine rage. PW confirms a literal supernatural threat; Library Journal calls it a triumph of folk horror. Community belief and its residents, not a haunted building or passive cursed ground, are the menace. Contemporary fantasy mystery fails the governing horror experience.

title: The Unworthy
rationale: Root-down: SF -> Futurist -> Future of Earth -> Dystopian futures -> Social dystopian future -> Patriarchal dystopias. After ecological collapse, a fundamentalist female sisterhood serves an unseen He through reproductive and bodily punishment, castes, mutilation and patriarchal discipline. Kirkus explicitly identifies patriarchy and compares The Handmaid's Tale. The regime's male rule persists through female enforcers; the surviving enclave and climate ruin provide context rather than the main engine. Publisher calls it dystopia and no literal deity or magic is established.

title: The Village at the Edge of Noon
rationale: Root-down: Fantasy -> Real earth fantasy -> Nocturne -> Dark -> Horror -> Unholy ground -> Cursed towns. A Russian dacha cooperative's exit disappears; its settlement is severed from reality, held in perpetual summer and besieged by Slavic supernatural neighbors. Katya's inherited power may rescue it. Belief and bargains help resist the menace but the people are not a cult enacting rites that create it: confinement and curse in the community's ground govern. A bounded cursed settlement, not a wilderness or building.

title: The Warden
rationale: Root-down: Fantasy realms -> Epic -> Heroic -> Caster heroes -> Mage hero. Graduate necromancer Aelis uses learned spellcraft as a rural warden to confront ancient evil. Tor calls it a non-stop action adventure; Locus centers her capable magical solutions. Cozy texture and community care do not govern the danger/adventure spine; formal education is backstory, not Magic school's present-day setting; necromancy alone is not Gothic engineering. First Warden-series card, not a separate card per sequel.

title: The Warm Hands of Ghosts
rationale: Root-down: Fantasy -> Real earth fantasy -> Historical -> Period -> Industrial age -> WWI fantasy. Laura returns to the Western Front seeking her brother after the 1917 Halifax explosion; Freddie and a German soldier escape the trenches into a devil's timeless hotel. Real ghosts and devil magic work inside the documented Great War stage. Not a rewritten historical fork, an occult explanation for known history or present-day war haunting; period anchoring governs over the deal-with-the-devil furniture.

reason: 1621 Denmark: Renaissance vs missing early-modern period boundary.

title: The West Passage
rationale: Root-down: Fantasy -> Fantasy realms -> Gothic fantasy -> Isolationist fantasy. The world is a sealed city-sized decaying palace, ruled by titanic Ladies and meaningless inherited rituals; two young custodians cross its towers to confront failing seasons and the Beast. Locus explicitly places it beside Gormenghast. Confinement, architecture and exhausted hierarchy govern, not an open-world epic quest, British manners, necromantic machinery or investigation. Invented-world fairy whimsy does not make this a revision of an identifiable prior fairy tale.

reason: New Weird endorsement, but root scientific biology vs literal magic remains unresolved.

title: These Burning Stars
rationale: Root-down: SF -> Futurist -> Spacefaring -> New space opera -> Political -> Interstellar court politics. Kindom religious hierarchy and First Families rule the interplanetary Treble; clerics, elite kin and a hacker pursue evidence of genocide through secret alliances and a revenge conspiracy. Religious institutions are political machinery rather than theological transcendence; private action serves elite power and intrigue rather than a mass revolutionary movement or simple adventure. First Kindom trilogy card.

title: Threads That Bind
rationale: Root-down: Fantasy -> Fantasy realms -> Gothic fantasy -> Fantasy mystery. Private detective Io investigates women made into supernatural assassins in half-sunken Alante, exposing occult lineage and monstrous institutional conspiracy. Locus identifies the noir investigation as the page-turning engine. Greek-derived divine ancestry supplies powers but this is not a retelling of named Greek myth nor contemporary real-Earth myth. The fated romance is subordinate to detection, not Romantasy. First card of the Threads That Bind/Hearts That Cut duology.

title: Tim Te Maro and the Subterranean Heartsick Blues
rationale: Root-down: Fantasy -> Real earth -> Contemporary -> Magical coming-of-age -> Magic school. At New Zealand's Fox Glacier High School for the Magically Adept, Tim and Elliott develop their relationship and identity through a formal class assignment caring for an enchanted egg that responds to their emotions. Magical school life provides the narrative structure, not an inherited-magic awakening or household fantasy. The real-Earth contemporary gate rejects secondary-world Romantasy despite romance being the emotional spine.

title: Titanium Noir
rationale: Root-down: SF -> Futurist -> Future of Earth -> Techno fiction -> Technomorphosis -> Posthuman -> Remade bodies. T7 gene therapy repeatedly rejuvenates the rich while enlarging them into physically different Titans. Their altered bodies, longevity and privileged power make the murder case possible. Publisher explicitly says near-future; Modern day's Genetic engineering and Technothriller fail that temporal gate. No magic, no mind upload or future-history panorama: bodily speciation is the novum under the noir investigation.

title: Toward Eternity
rationale: Root-down: SF -> Futurist -> Future of Earth -> Techno -> Technomorphosis -> Posthuman -> Remade bodies. Cancer treatment replaces every cell with nanites, making nanodroid people whose bodies reproduce and change humanity across eons. Patient One disappears and returns, an AI gains a body through the same process, and patient-derived doubles spread. Consciousness and love are explored through embodiment and synthetic cellular replacement, not uploading minds to a digital world. Bodily/species transformation governs over future-history panorama or machine personhood alone. Tenth card: leaf freezes for split priority.

title: Transmentation | Transience
rationale: Root-down: SF -> Atemporal -> Parallel world fiction -> Multiverse war. Minds transfer into proxies across scientific parallel realities; Burel Hird's imperial control, a violent diplomatic incident and rival pan-dimensional societies drive espionage and conflict. Embodied identity is explored through the crossing, but political conquest between worlds is its purpose, not an intimate multiverse odyssey or mirrored Earth counterfactual. No literal magic established despite fantasy-like localities.

title: Under the Eye of the Big Bird
rationale: Root-down: SF -> Futurist -> Future of Earth -> Techno -> Technomorphosis -> Posthuman -> Remade bodies. Engineered human descendants combine animal DNA, plant nutrition and accelerated breeding across fourteen far-future communities; AI Mothers and watchers attempt to jumpstart evolution against genetic extinction. The designed organism/species is the experiment, not mind uploading or barren childless society. Geological scope supports future history, but bodily redesign and what counts as humanity govern; no actual travel through time or literal magic is established.

title: Unraveller
rationale: Root-down: Fantasy realms -> Epic -> Heroic -> Caster heroes -> Mage hero. Kellen's unique direct mastery unravels curses, driving a journey through Raddith's towns, markets and Deep Wilds alongside formerly cursed Nettle. Investigation is necessary to undo each curse, but the caster's magical power, ethical growth and adventures are the spine, not a Gothic detective institution, military campaign or political overthrow. Not inherited Earth magic, a revision of a named fairy tale or an explicit system-building epic.

reason: 1840s border vampires: Monsters in Gaslight vs Weird West.

title: Vanishing World
rationale: Root-down: SF -> Historical -> Alternate history -> Period alterations -> Alt postwar. PW explicitly anchors artificial insemination's rapid development to WWII; Amane lives in the changed postwar Japan where sex is taboo and Experiment City makes parenthood collective. A WWII fork within the generation preceding the depicted adulthood satisfies Alt postwar, not undated future dystopia or unanchored fabulation. Deep alterations is less exact because the named WWII-period fork and its immediate social legacy govern. Scientific reproduction, no literal magic.

title: Waterblack
reason: Cities of the Weft trilogy finale, publisher/review confirms existing Mordew series card. Preserve existing classification; no new card.
1980s conscious generative-literature computer: Period SF era gap; Written worlds not established.

title: We Lived on the Horizon
rationale: Root-down: SF -> Futurist -> Future of Earth -> Techno fiction -> Machine minds -> Robots -> Sentient robots. Enita builds her personal AI Nix a body and the narrative explores its divergent consciousness, bodily autonomy and claim to personhood during Bulwark's class revolt. Author and Locus center the surgeon and embodied AI rather than revolution organizers. Parallax's distributed city intelligence is context; Nix's body and becoming someone govern, not indistinguishable-human passing, generalized surveillance or the class struggle alone.

title: Bunny
rationale: Root-down: Fantasy -> Real earth -> Earthly comic fantasy. MFA students form a coven and turn real rabbits into imperfect male Darlings/Drafts, a literal supernatural workshop used for savage academic satire. We Love You, Bunny revisits the same coven, protagonist and created First Boy, expanding the shared events; coalesced on the first book's card. Kirkus centers hilarious grotesquerie and satire. Not SF Written worlds: drafting is figurative language for physical witchcraft, not proof the world is made of text, and literal magic excludes the SF side.

title: When Devils Sing
rationale: Root-down: Fantasy -> Real earth -> Nocturne -> Supernatural -> Evil deals -> Deal with the devil. Carrion's prosperity and class divide arise from a founding bargain demanding sacrifice every thirteen-year cicada emergence; Sam also bargains with a demon to save her brother. The Devil and his human servants make supernatural contracts the mechanism. Cursed town and Folk horror are strong atmosphere matches, but a named devil's bargain does the work rather than an impersonal ground curse or autonomous community rite.

title: Where Peace Is Lost
rationale: Root-down: SF -> Futurist -> Spacefaring -> New space opera -> Space adventure. Refugee Kel guides two offworlders through Loth's jungle to disable an awakened war machine, protecting the locals while concealing her identity. The action quest, physical danger and mismatched companions govern. Imperial war is past context rather than a military campaign or organized revolution; apparent paladin/sword furniture is technological, with no actual magic established.

title: Wicked Problems
reason: Craft Wars book 2, direct sequel to Dead Country. Publisher and author identify series; preserve existing Technomancy card.

title: Womb City
rationale: Root-down: Fantasy -> Real earth -> Nocturne -> Dark -> Torment -> Vengeance torment. After Nelah kills Moremi to hide an affair, Moremi's literal vengeful ghost stalks her and demands her loved ones as reparation; Botswana ancestral folklore and a ritual conspiracy govern the second half. Body-hopping technology and surveillance initially look like SF, but Locus and Reactor explicitly identify the supernatural ghost engine. No magic on the SF side: cyberpunk bodies are furniture, not an excuse to shelve a literal haunting as technological consciousness transfer.

title: Wrath Goddess Sing
rationale: Root-down: Fantasy -> Real earth -> Mythic retelling -> Greek myth fantasy. Trans-woman Achilles is transformed by Athena and enters the Trojan War against a powerful Helen; the Iliad's named figures and inherited myth form the source and plot. Not chronicle-based Period fantasy, modern myth persisting in contemporary life or an invented-world heroic quest. Divine intervention is literal and mythic-age retelling is the exact branch.

title: Written on the Dark
rationale: Root-down: Fantasy -> Fantasy realms -> Epic -> Political -> Court intrigue -> Court spies. In two-moon Ferrieres, poet Thierry Villar is recruited as a tavern informant after the king's brother is murdered, uncovering a conspiracy and usurpation plot as war approaches. Kay's veiled fifteenth-century France is an invented world, not documented Earth. Covert information, assassination and manipulation around the court govern rather than ruler-level governance or claimant-centered dynastic legitimacy; the medieval furniture does not outrank about-ness.

title: Ymir
rationale: Root-down: SF -> Futurist -> Spacefaring -> New space opera -> Space adventure. Corporate hunter-killer Yorick returns to icy mining planet Ymir to kill an alien technological grendel, is coerced by his brother into sabotage and must survive violent reversals. PW identifies nonstop action, Locus the compressed few-days momentum. The anti-company plot and estranged family supply stakes, but physical danger and the hunt govern, not a broad imperial revolution, social dystopia or exploration of an alien megastructure. Beowulf is inspiration, not literal Norse myth.
